paragraphs: So on that frosty, snowy, windy Sunday in November, Kolya Krassotkin sat at home. There was no school. It had just struck eleven, and he badly wanted to go out “on very urgent business.” But he had been left alone in charge of the house, since every one of the grown-ups was away because of a sudden and unusual event. Madame Krassotkin rented two small rooms, cut off from the rest of the house by a passage, to a doctor’s wife and her two small children. This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna and a great friend of hers. Her husband, the doctor, had gone away twelve months before, first to Orenburg and then to Tashkend, and for the past six months she had heard nothing from him. Without her friendship with Madame Krassotkin, which was some comfort to the abandoned wife, she would surely have dissolved completely in tears. And now, on top of her troubles, her only servant, Katerina, had announced the evening before, to her mistress’s amazement, that she planned to have a baby before morning. It seemed almost miraculous to everyone that nobody had seen this coming. The astounded doctor’s wife decided to move Katerina, while there was still time, to a house in town kept by a midwife for just such emergencies. She thought a great deal of her servant, so she did this at once and stayed there to look after her. By morning, Madame Krassotkin’s friendly sympathy and energy were all needed, to help out and to find someone to turn to in the matter.

So both ladies were out of the house, the Krassotkins’ servant, Agafya, had gone to the market, and Kolya had been left for a while to guard and look after “the kids,” the doctor’s wife’s son and daughter, who were alone there. Kolya wasn’t afraid to mind the house. Besides, he had Perezvon, who had been told to lie flat under the bench in the hall and not move. Each time Kolya, pacing through the rooms, came into the hall, the dog shook his head and thumped the floor twice with his tail, loudly and with a hint. But alas! The whistle that would let him go never came. Kolya gave the luckless dog a stern look, and the dog sank back into obedient stiffness. The one thing that troubled Kolya was “the kids.” He regarded Katerina’s unexpected adventure, of course, with the utmost scorn, but he was very fond of the bereaved “kiddies,” and he had already brought them a picture-book. Nastya, the elder, was eight and could read, and Kostya, the boy, was seven and loved being read to by her. Krassotkin could, of course, have found more entertaining things to do with them. He could have made them stand side by side and played soldiers, or sent them hiding all over the house. He had done it more than once, and he wasn’t above doing it. In fact, a story once went around school that Krassotkin played horses with the little lodgers at home, prancing with his head to one side like a trace-horse. But Krassotkin haughtily parried the jab. To play horses with boys his own age, boys of thirteen, he said, would certainly be disgraceful “at this date.” But he did it for “the kids,” because he liked them, and nobody had a right to call him to account for his feelings. The two “kids” adored him.

This time, though, he was in no mood for games. He had very important business of his own ahead, something almost mysterious. Meanwhile time was passing, and Agafya, the one he could have left the children with, still hadn’t come back from the market. Several times already he had crossed the passage, opened the door of the lodgers’ room and looked in anxiously at “the kids,” who were sitting over the book, as he had told them to. Every time he opened the door they grinned at him, hoping he would come in and do something delightful and amusing. But Kolya was worried, and he didn’t go in.

Finally it struck eleven, and he decided, once and for all, that if that “damned” Agafya wasn’t back in ten minutes, he would go out without her. Of course he would first make “the kids” promise to be brave while he was gone, not to be naughty, and not to cry from fright. With that in mind he put on his wadded winter overcoat with the catskin collar and slung his satchel over his shoulder. His mother was always begging him to wear galoshes in such cold weather. He ignored her pleas; he gave the galoshes a scornful glance as he crossed the hall and went out in his boots alone. Perezvon, seeing him in his outdoor clothes, started drumming nervously but hard on the floor with his tail. He twitched all over and even let out a plaintive whine. But Kolya, seeing the dog’s passionate excitement, decided that this was a breach of discipline. He kept him under the bench for one more minute, and only after opening the door into the passage did he whistle for him. The dog sprang up like a madman and rushed bounding ahead of him, wild with joy.

Kolya opened the door to peep in at “the kids.” They were both sitting at the table as before, not reading now but arguing warmly about something. The children often argued together about the exciting problems of life, and Nastya, being older, always won. If Kostya didn’t agree with her, he nearly always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and both of them took his verdict as final. This time the “kids’” debate interested Krassotkin rather a lot, and he stopped in the passage to listen. The children saw that he was listening, and that made them argue with even more energy.

“I’ll never, never believe,” Nastya prattled, “that old women find babies in the cabbage patch. It’s winter now and there aren’t any cabbages, so the old woman couldn’t have brought Katerina a daughter.”
Kolya whistled softly to himself.
“Or maybe they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to people who are married.”
Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, thinking it over very deeply.
“Oh, Nastya, you’re so silly!” he said at last, firmly and calmly. “How can Katerina have a baby if she isn’t married?”
Nastya was exasperated.
“You know nothing about it,” she snapped irritably. “Maybe she has a husband, only he’s in prison, and so now she’s got a baby.”
“But is her husband in prison?” asked the matter-of-fact Kostya, gravely.

“Or, I’ll tell you what,” Nastya broke in impulsively, completely throwing out and forgetting her first guess. “She hasn’t got a husband, you’re right about that, but she wants to be married, and so she’s been thinking about getting married, and thinking and thinking about it, till now she’s got it, that is, not a husband but a baby.”
“Well, maybe,” Kostya agreed, totally beaten. “But you didn’t say that before. How was I supposed to know?”
“Come on, kiddies,” said Kolya, stepping into the room. “You’re terrible people, I can see.”
“And Perezvon’s with you!” Kostya grinned, and he started snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.
“I’ve got a problem, kids,” Krassotkin began solemnly, “and you have to help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she still hasn’t turned up. That’s certain. I have to go out. Will you let me?”
The children looked anxiously at each other. Their smiling faces grew uneasy, but they didn’t yet quite understand what was wanted of them.
“You won’t be naughty while I’m gone? You won’t climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won’t get scared by yourselves and cry?”
A look of deep gloom came over the children’s faces.
“And I could show you something as a reward, a little copper cannon that you can fire with real gunpowder.”
The children’s faces lit up at once. “Show us the cannon,” said Kostya, beaming all over.
Krassotkin reached into his satchel, took out a little bronze cannon and stood it on the table.
“Ah, I knew you’d ask! Look, it’s on wheels.” He rolled the toy along the table. “And you can fire it, too. You load it with shot and fire it off.”
“And it could kill somebody?”

“It could kill anybody; you just have to aim at him,” and Krassotkin showed them where the powder went in and where the shot was rolled in. He pointed out a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them it kicked back when fired.
The children listened with great interest. What fired their imagination most was that the cannon kicked.
“And have you got powder?” Nastya asked.
“I have.”
“Show us the powder, too,” she drawled, smiling to coax him.

Krassotkin dived into his satchel again and brought out a small flask with a little real gunpowder in it. He had some shot, too, in a twist of paper. He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into the palm of his hand.
“You have to make sure there’s no fire anywhere near, or it will blow up and kill us all,” Krassotkin warned them, making the most of it.
The children stared at the powder with an awestruck fear that only added to their enjoyment. But Kostya liked the shot better.
“Does shot burn?” he asked.
“No, it doesn’t.”
“Give me a bit of shot,” he begged, in a pleading voice.
“I’ll give you a bit of shot; here, take it. But don’t show it to your mother till I’m back, or she’ll be sure to think it’s gunpowder, and she’ll die of fright and give you a thrashing.”
“Mother never whips us,” Nastya said right away.
“I know, I only said that to round off the sentence. And never deceive your mother, except this one time, till I get back. So, kiddies, can I go out? You won’t be frightened and cry when I’m gone?”
“We sha—all cry,” Kostya drawled, already close to tears.
“We’ll cry, we’re sure to cry,” Nastya chimed in, hurriedly and timidly.
“Oh, children, children, how full of peril your years are! It can’t be helped, chickens, I’ll have to stay with you, goodness knows how long. And time is passing, time is passing, oogh!”
“Tell Perezvon to play dead!” Kostya begged.
“It can’t be helped, we’ll have to turn to Perezvon. _Ici_, Perezvon.” And Kolya started giving the dog orders, and the dog went through all his tricks.

He was a rough-haired dog, of middle size, with a coat of a sort of lilac-gray color. He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn. He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, and lay on his back with his paws in the air, stiff as if he were dead. In the middle of this last trick the door opened, and in the doorway appeared Agafya, Madame Krassotkin’s servant, a stout woman of forty with a pockmarked face. She was back from the market with a bag full of groceries in her hand. She held the bag up in her left hand and stood there watching the dog. Kolya had been so impatient for her return, but he didn’t cut the show short. He kept Perezvon dead for the usual time, and only then did he whistle to him. The dog leapt up and began bounding about, happy to have done his duty.
“Fancy that, a dog!” Agafya remarked, in her pompous way.
“Why are you late, female?” Krassotkin asked sternly.
“Female, indeed! Go on with you, you brat.”
“Brat?”

“Yes, a brat. What business is it of yours if I’m late? If I’m late, you can be sure I had good reason,” muttered Agafya, bustling around the stove, without a trace of anger or annoyance in her voice. She seemed quite pleased, in fact, to have a bit of a squabble with her cheerful young master.

“Listen, you frivolous young person,” Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, “can you swear by everything you hold sacred in the world, and something more besides, that you’ll keep a careful eye on the kids while I’m out? I’m going out.”
“And what would I swear for?” Agafya laughed. “I’ll look after them without that.”
“No, you have to swear on your eternal salvation. Or else I’m not going.”
“Well, don’t, then. What do I care? It’s cold out; stay home.”

“Kids,” Kolya said, turning to the children, “this woman will stay with you till I’m back or till your mother comes, since she should have been home long ago. She’ll give you lunch, too. You’ll give them something, Agafya, won’t you?”
“That much I can do.”

“Goodbye, chickens, I’m leaving with an easy mind. And you, granny,” he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, “I hope you’ll have pity on their tender years and not fill their heads with any of your old wives’ nonsense about Katerina. _Ici_, Perezvon!”
“Get out with you!” retorted Agafya, really angry this time. “What a ridiculous boy! You need a whipping for saying such things, that’s what you need!”
